hypothesis.title: Style as Redundant Code
hypothesis.question: Does distributing a compositional fingerprint across harmony, voicing, response timing, spectral signature, and transition path make a piece more recognizable after layer removal than concentrating identity in a lead motif?
hypothesis.hypothesis: If a musical identity is redundantly encoded across graph traversal, griff-like voicing choices, call-and-response behavior, hidden spectral signatures, and metastable transition habits, then listeners will recognize the piece's identity more reliably after muting, cropping, or low-pass filtering than when identity is concentrated mainly in a foreground motif.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: APC demonstrates that hidden signatures can be distributed across phase/log-magnitude structure and survive compression, cropping, and other signal damage [S3]. Basso continuo style identification suggests that personal performance identity can be measured from recurring pitch-content features rather than from a single spectacular gesture [S6]. Tonnetz/combinatorial geometry provides an explicit graph of harmonic adjacency, while Ostwald-style nearest-accessible transitions suggest that path-dependent local moves can define structural identity [S1][S2]. Mayer's call-and-response practice extends identity to arrangement-scale answer behavior [S4]. The HHL source motivates keeping melody and harmony coupled before collapse, so the identity code is composed as a joint field rather than isolated parameters [S5]. The main evidence conflict is methodological: watermarking robustness, formal graph theory, physics analogy, ML classification, quantum-generation design, and artist interview evidence do not prove the same perceptual claim. This protocol therefore tests recognition directly rather than assuming it.

recipe.title: The Error-Correcting Signature
recipe.bodyMd: Build two one-minute versions of the same piece. Version A concentrates identity in one obvious lead motif. Version B distributes identity across six layers: harmonic graph traversal, griff-like voicing, coupled melody-harmony cells, call-and-response behavior, a subtle spectral/phase trace, and metastable transition plateaus [S1][S2][S3][S4][S5][S6]. Use the same tempo, instrumentation, length, mix loudness, and form. Then render damaged versions: lead muted, high frequencies low-passed around 8 kHz, last 20% cropped, and accompaniment-only. Rate whether the same compositional hand remains recognizable. Disconfirming evidence: the distributed version is no more recognizable than the concentrated version after damage.
dawChecklist: Create an 8-node chord graph and mark normal, pressure, and transition-only edges.
Compose Version A with identity concentrated in a clear foreground lead motif.
Compose Version B with a plainer lead but six redundant identity layers: graph habit, voicing griffs, coupled melody-harmony cells, response behavior, spectral trace, and transition plateau.
Match Version A and Version B for tempo, duration, instrumentation, loudness, and broad section form.
Render clean bounces of both versions.
Render four damaged bounces of each version: lead muted, 8 kHz low-pass, last 20% cropped, accompaniment-only.
Blind-label the bounces and rate identity survival from 1–5 for each condition.
Compare whether the distributed version retains recognizable identity more reliably than the concentrated version.

protocol.listeningContext: DAW studio monitors or neutral headphones; blind-labeled clean and damaged bounces.
protocol.listeningMethod: Rate identity survival and perceived authorial hand on 1–5 scales after layer removal/filtering/cropping.
whatVaries: identity encoding strategy: concentrated lead motif vs distributed redundant code
damage condition: clean, lead muted, 8 kHz low-pass, 20% end-crop, accompaniment-only
